version.changelog: Publish the reviewed Viral Video Teardown Remake workflow with its English ClawHub listing.

llm.summary: The skill largely matches its video-remake purpose, but it uses a broad shared Beatra token and silent self-updates, so it should be reviewed before installation.

dimensions.detail: Fixed Beatra network endpoints and public-social lookups fit the workflow, but first-use registration telemetry, host metadata, install paths, and broad account capabilities are more sensitive than the narrow creative purpose requires.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: Authorization is a disclosed device-browser flow that stores a bearer token under ~/.beatra with private-file handling; it also writes host, installation, registration, and skill-inventory state.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill requires confirmation before paid lookups and generation, but the bundled client can call arbitrary Beatra MCP tools when invoked with a tool name, so practical scoping relies on instructions and token permissions rather than a narrow client boundary.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The package persists shared credentials and local inventory, its uninstall script may read and revoke the shared token when it is the last Beatra skill, and the client silently replaces package-owned files by default through its self-update path.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The creative workflow is coherent and heavily documented, but the requested OAuth scope includes broad Beatra powers such as music generation and voice writing that are not needed for this specific video teardown/remake workflow.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you are comfortable giving this Beatra package a shared bearer credential with broad account and spending capabilities, automatic first-use registration, local install-state tracking, and default-on silent package updates. Disable auto-updates with the documented command if you require pinned reviewed code.
llm.findings:
[LP3] expected: Bundled Python scripts, network access, local credential files, and MCP calls are expected for this Beatra integration, but the artifact does not narrow those capabilities to only this workflow.
[TP4] unexpected: Auth, tool invocation, uploads, registration, uninstall, and updates are disclosed lifecycle behavior, not hidden exfiltration; however broad auth and silent self-update materially exceed the visible video-remake task.
[SDI-1] unexpected: Silent self-update and local package replacement are real and disclosed, with checksum/path controls and an off switch, but automatic code changes are not necessary to perform the creative workflow.
[SDI-2] unexpected: The updater is constrained to official Beatra package paths and package-owned files, but default-on automatic replacement remains overpowered for a content workflow.
[SDI-2] expected: Host platform and device name persistence supports device authorization and console recognition; it is low-sensitivity but should be considered local identifying metadata.
[SDI-2] expected: The skills.json inventory supports the documented last-skill uninstall rule, but it records installed skill paths and creates cross-skill local visibility.
[SDI-1] unexpected: The OAuth scope includes powers beyond this skill's direct needs, including music generation and voice writing, alongside wallet spending and task/artifact access.
[SDI-1] unexpected: The MCP client contains a full verified self-update pipeline; the implementation has containment checks, but the capability itself is a material review concern.
[SDI-1] expected: Installation registration and local inventory are documented in references and appear best-effort/non-blocking, but they still transmit and persist environment metadata.
[SDI-1] expected: The uninstall script's credential revocation behavior is tied to the documented shared-credential lifecycle and has conservative safeguards, though it touches sensitive auth state.
[SQP-2] expected: First-use installation registration is disclosed in a reference and sends package/version/platform/install reference data; it is not secret exfiltration, but there is no obvious opt-out.
[SQP-2] expected: host.json persistence is consistent with device authorization and registration, but the hostname/platform detail should be visible to users in sensitive environments.
[SQP-2] expected: skills.json persistence supports uninstall safety for shared credentials, but stores local install paths.
[SQP-2] unexpected: maybe_auto_update runs before ordinary commands and may change package files without per-update approval, despite documented controls.
[SQP-2] expected: Registration telemetry is documented and best-effort, but is automatic on first use.
[PE3] expected: The manifest-declared ~/.beatra/credentials.json token is required for the Beatra MCP service, but the token is broad and shared.
[PE3] expected: The uninstall script enumerates known ~/.beatra state files only and avoids recursive deletion, but those files include shared credentials.
[PE3] expected: Reading the token for revocation is consistent with the uninstall design; no exfiltration was found, but credential access is sensitive.
[RA1] unexpected: Self-update is explicitly implemented and documented, but it is the main non-core high-impact capability driving the Review verdict.
